page12_img_table_1.png.title: Meta‑Work AI systems: documentation, onboarding, communications, and discovery
page12_img_table_1.png.description: A four-row table summarizing the Meta‑Work category (Table 6) that maps four desired AI systems to the problems they address, example capability steps, and the constraints developers insist on. The systems are: DocSync (continuous documentation synchronizer) to detect drift and generate targeted doc patches but only as human‑approved drafts that do not fabricate missing rationale; a Contextualized Developer Ramp‑Up Coach that builds personalized onboarding playbooks and hands‑on exercises while explicitly not replacing human mentoring and surfacing uncertainty; a Stakeholder Communication Draft Workbench that extracts facts and drafts audience‑calibrated messages but must never send communications or handle relationship‑critical content automatically; and an Interactive Exploration Board for early tech discovery that generates multiple option cards with assumptions yet must not inject unsolicited design decisions and requires human validation. Across rows, recurring guardrails appear: outputs remain drafts, provenance and citations are required, uncertainty must be signaled, and human judgment and mentorship remain the final authority.

page2_img_1.png.title: Grounded taxonomy of SE task categories with example tasks
page2_img_1.png.description: A two-column table mapping five high-level software engineering categories to exemplar tasks used in the survey. Categories are: Development (coding/programming; bug fixing/debugging; performance optimization; refactoring & maintenance/updates; AI integration), Design & Planning (system design, requirements engineering, project planning & management), Quality & Risk Management (testing & quality assurance; code review/pull requests; security & compliance), Infrastructure & Operations (DevOps/CI‑CD; environment setup & maintenance; infrastructure monitoring; customer support), and Meta‑work (Collaboration/Knowledge Building) (documentation; client/stakeholder communication; mentoring & onboarding; learning; research & brainstorming). This taxonomy framed which task blocks participants selected and informed the open‑ended questions that produced the 22 desired AI systems described in the paper.

page7_img_table_1.png.title: Design & Planning AI systems: tasks, capabilities, and guardrails
page7_img_table_1.png.description: A three-column table listing five AI systems developers want for Design & Planning, each row showing (1) the system name, (2) the problem it addresses, (3) example capability steps, and (4) constraints and guardrails. The five systems (with prevalence in the survey noted in the paper) are: Design-to-sprint workbench (30.5%) — generating work breakdowns, dependency maps, and milestone sequences from an accepted design; Architecture studio for requirements-to-design (27.8%) — creating a persistent design state from ADRs and infra catalogs and producing distinct architecture candidates; Design analyzer for trade-off and risk (20.6%) — mapping designs to requirements, surfacing hidden dependencies, and producing what‑if trade-offs; Decision context and provenance graph (19.7%) — extracting dated decisions and linking them to source artifacts; and Full-loop design doc and diagram workbench (15.2%) — turning notes and diffs into editable docs and diagrams. Across all rows the table emphasizes the same constraints: every output must remain human-gated (no final decisions, no autonomous plan changes or deployments), provenance and source context must be exposed, uncertainty must be signaled, and the system must avoid fabricating missing requirements or sensitive data exposure.

page6_img_table_1.png.title: Four AI systems developers want for Development work
page6_img_table_1.png.description: A four-column table summarizing four AI systems requested by developers in the Development block (N=353), with columns for the system name, the problem it addresses, example capabilities, and constraints/guardrails. The rows correspond to: (1) Scoped-PR builder for tech-debt removal (50.1%) — addressing large, brittle refactors by proposing small, reviewable atomic diffs; (2) Embedded quality gate for code and tests (27.8%) — providing diff-anchored error and coverage feedback before a PR is opened; (3) Trace-to-diff root-cause workbench (19.5%) — automating evidence collection, failure timelines, and hypothesis generation for incidents; and (4) Repository context graph for cross-file changes (18.4%) — maintaining a persistent code-and-history graph to compute impact reports for proposed edits. Example capabilities emphasize deriving minimal impacted areas, attaching rationale from PR discussions/ADRs, generating succinct quality reports or patches, and producing reproducible failure timelines; recurring constraints require explicit human approval (no automatic commits or one-shot refactors), explicit uncertainty/provenance signaling, sandboxed reproduction, and flagging missing domain context rather than inventing it.

page4_img_1.png.title: Human-in-the-loop multi-model thematic analysis pipeline
page4_img_1.png.description: A flowchart of the analysis pipeline used to extract themes from survey responses, drawn as two parallel tracks: an Opportunity Track (blue) for “want” themes and a Constraint Track (brown) for “not want” themes. For each track three models independently perform Independent Theme Discovery, then GPT‑5.2 performs Reconciliation to merge candidate themes into a unified codebook. That codebook passes through a Human Gate labeled Author Review & Codebook Approval (researchers validate, split/merge/update/delete themes and add positive/negative examples), after which the three models run Systematic Coding (rationale-first, batch = 20) on every response. The final Triangulation step computes inter-rater reliability (Krippendorff’s α per theme), applies a 2-of-3 majority-vote consensus, and aggregates ISSUE_* data-quality flags, emphasizing model diversity, auditable rationales, and human oversight.

page11_img_table_1.png.title: Infrastructure & Ops AI systems: problems, capabilities, and guardrails
page11_img_table_1.png.description: This table summarizes four AI systems 101 respondents wanted for Infrastructure & Operations, pairing the problem each addresses with example capability steps and strict constraints. Telemetry correlation assistant (requested by ~40.6% of infra respondents) would assemble compact evidence bundles from correlated telemetry, suggest alert tuning (thresholds, deduplication), update dependency graphs, and produce a structured incident brief; the CI/CD & IaC blueprint builder (~33.7%) would parse repositories into delivery profiles, build topology maps of CI/CD stages, and generate reproducible pipeline skeletons and staged migration diffs. The maintenance backlog prioritizer (~16.8%) would normalize deprecation/security/runtime signals into a prioritized remediation queue with rationale, and the customer support triage assistant (~11.9%) would organize tickets, redact sensitive fields, retrieve similar resolved cases, and draft triage cards for review. Across all four rows the table emphasizes common guardrails: read-only/default no-write access, no autonomous production actions or approvals, reproducible/inspectable outputs, strict privacy controls (no raw customer data handling), and explicit human oversight for any change.
